options.why: Directionally better, since allow-listing beats deny-listing, and AST filtering is a reasonable extra layer. But in-process AST restriction has been repeatedly broken, and a bug in your filter is still full compromise — the boundary is in the same process either way.

explanation: The principle is that a deny-list encodes what you thought of and an allow-list encodes what you need, so any security control based on enumerating bad things loses to an adversary — or an unlucky model — with more imagination than you. In-process execution is worse still, because the code shares your credentials, environment variables, network access and memory. Even without malice, a generated infinite loop or memory exhaustion takes down the service. The alternative is a genuine isolation boundary. Containers with a read-only root filesystem, a dropped capability set, no network namespace, memory and CPU limits, and a hard timeout cover most internal uses. For untrusted or user-supplied code, go further to gVisor or a microVM such as Firecracker, which is what the commercial code-execution sandboxes use. Then design what crosses the boundary deliberately: input data mounted read-only, output collected from a specific path or stdout, no ambient credentials, and network access denied by default with a narrow allow-list if genuinely needed. Add the operational controls that make it safe to run: per-execution resource limits so one job cannot starve others, a fresh sandbox per execution so state cannot leak between users, and full logging of code and output for audit. And note that this is a case where the pragmatic answer is often to buy rather than build — sandboxing is a specialised and unforgiving problem, and a managed code-execution service is usually cheaper than getting it wrong once.
keyTakeaway: Deny-lists enumerate what you imagined; isolation enumerates what you allow. Untrusted code belongs in a container or microVM, never in-process.

stem: You want to measure a RAG system properly. Which set of metrics gives you an actionable picture, and why is end-to-end answer quality alone insufficient?

options.text: Retrieval recall@k, context precision, groundedness, and answer relevance — because a single end-to-end score tells you quality moved but not which stage caused it
options.why: Each metric isolates one stage, so a drop points at a specific fix. An aggregate score conflates a retrieval miss, a ranking problem and an ungrounded generation into one number that gives you nothing to act on.

options.text: BLEU and ROUGE against reference answers, since they are standard and reproducible
options.why: N-gram overlap metrics reward surface similarity to one particular phrasing, which correlates poorly with correctness for open-ended answers. A correct answer worded differently scores badly and a fluent wrong one can score well.

options.text: User thumbs-up rate and session length, since they reflect real satisfaction
options.why: Product signals worth collecting, but they are sparse, biased toward users who bother to rate, and lagging. They also cannot localise a fault — a falling thumbs-up rate tells you something broke, not what.

options.text: Latency, cost per query, and token counts, since quality is subjective
options.why: Operational metrics you certainly need, and treating quality as unmeasurable is the assumption that keeps teams shipping blind. Quality is measurable with graded rubrics and component metrics; declaring it subjective just means nobody is accountable for it.

explanation: RAG is a pipeline, and pipeline metrics must be per stage or you cannot act on them. The four that matter: retrieval recall@k, whether the chunk containing the answer was fetched at all — this sets the ceiling for everything downstream and is measured against a labelled set of question-to-chunk pairs; context precision, what fraction of retrieved chunks are actually relevant, since distractors dilute attention and cost tokens; groundedness or faithfulness, whether every claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved context, which is the hallucination measure and the one that catches confident wrongness; and answer relevance, whether the answer addresses the question asked, which catches grounded but unhelpful responses. Together these localise faults: low recall means fix chunking, embeddings or hybrid search; good recall with low precision means add a reranker; good context with low groundedness means fix the generation prompt; everything good but low relevance means the model is answering a different question. Two practices that make this real. Build the labelled set from your own documents by generating candidate questions per chunk and having a human verify a sample — you need a few hundred pairs, not thousands, and it is a day's work that pays back permanently. And run these on every change to any stage, since the stages interact: a chunking change alters what retrieval can find, and a retrieval change alters what generation must handle.
keyTakeaway: Measure recall@k, context precision, groundedness and answer relevance separately. One end-to-end score cannot tell you which stage broke.

references.label: Es et al., 'RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation'

stem: This is the safety layer for a customer-facing assistant. What is the main weakness?

options.text: All enforcement is in the prompt, which is a probabilistic request — there is no independent check on input or output that can actually block a violation
options.why: A system prompt shapes behaviour but cannot enforce it, and a sufficiently unusual or adversarial input will get past it. Without a separate check outside the model, nothing in this design can prevent a violating response from reaching the customer.

options.text: The instructions are negative, and models follow positive instructions more reliably
options.why: A real prompt-engineering point — describing what to do generally beats a list of prohibitions — and rewriting would help at the margin. But better phrasing of an unenforceable instruction is still unenforceable.

options.text: There is no conversation history, so the assistant cannot maintain context across turns
options.why: A functional gap that would make the product feel broken, and history would need adding. It is a capability omission rather than the safety weakness the question asks about.

options.text: The system prompt is too short to define the assistant's scope adequately
options.why: More detail about scope and tone would improve behaviour, and scope restriction is genuinely one of the better mitigations. But length is not the issue — the issue is that the only control point is inside the model.

explanation: Guardrails need a control point outside the model, because instructions to a model are requests rather than constraints. Build three layers. Input checks run before the model: classify for prohibited topics, detect obvious injection attempts, and reject or route the request — this is cheap and catches a lot. Output checks run after generation and before the response reaches the user: verify against policy with a classifier or rules, check for leaked system prompt content, verify claims against retrieved sources where the answer should be grounded, and block or regenerate on failure. And structural constraints remove the possibility rather than discouraging it: if the assistant must never give financial advice, restrict it to retrieval over an approved document set and refuse anything not answerable from it, which is a far stronger control than an instruction. Keep the system prompt too — it is a real and useful layer, just not the only one. Two operational points. Design what happens when a guardrail fires: a safe fallback message, a log entry, and a metric, since a guardrail with no telemetry gives you no idea whether it fires ten times a day or ten thousand. And accept the false-positive cost explicitly, because an over-aggressive filter that blocks legitimate questions is its own product failure — tune the threshold with the same eval discipline you apply to quality. Note that streaming complicates output checks, since you cannot unshow shown tokens, which is a real architectural constraint to decide early.
keyTakeaway: A system prompt is a request, not a control. Put checks on input and output outside the model, and remove capabilities rather than forbidding them.

references.label: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications

stem: Search results contain documents that are topically related but do not answer the question — a query about 'how to cancel a subscription' returns the page about 'how to upgrade a subscription'. What does this reveal about embedding similarity?

options.text: Embeddings measure semantic relatedness, not answer-ness — 'cancel' and 'upgrade' are close in the space because they share topic and structure
options.why: Embedding similarity captures distributional and topical closeness, and antonyms or alternatives appear in near-identical contexts, so they embed close together. Nothing in the objective distinguishes 'about the same subject' from 'answers this question'.

options.text: The embedding model is undertrained on your domain and needs fine-tuning
options.why: Domain adaptation does help and is worth doing for specialised vocabulary. But this specific confusion is inherent to how similarity works — even a perfectly domain-tuned model places 'cancel' and 'upgrade' near each other for the same structural reason.

options.text: Cosine similarity is the wrong metric; dot product or Euclidean distance would separate these
options.why: For normalised vectors cosine and dot product are equivalent ranking functions, and Euclidean is monotonically related. Changing the metric does not change which vectors are near each other, so the confusion survives.

options.text: The chunks are too large, so multiple topics are mixed within one embedding
options.why: Multi-topic chunks do produce muddied, averaged embeddings and smaller chunks would sharpen retrieval. That is a different problem though — here the pages are correctly about distinct single topics and are still confused.

explanation: Embeddings place text near other text that appears in similar contexts, which makes them excellent at topical association and poor at distinctions that matter for answering. Antonyms are the clearest case: 'cancel' and 'upgrade' appear in almost identical sentences, so the space cannot separate them on the axis you care about. Negation is similarly invisible — 'this feature is supported' and 'this feature is not supported' embed very close. The practical response is layered. Add a cross-encoder reranker over the retrieved candidates, which scores query and document jointly rather than independently and can therefore represent the interaction that a single similarity score cannot; this is the highest-value single addition to most retrieval stacks and typically fixes exactly this symptom. Use hybrid retrieval so lexical matching contributes the exact terms. Where the corpus supports it, add metadata filters so an intent classifier can restrict to cancellation documents. And consider embedding a hypothetical question for each chunk alongside its text, which aligns the representation with how users actually query rather than how documents are written. One further point worth carrying: do not compare similarity scores across different embedding models or assume a fixed threshold generalises — the scale is model-specific and unstable, so tune thresholds per model against your own labelled set rather than adopting a number from a blog post.
keyTakeaway: Embeddings encode topical relatedness, so antonyms and negation land close together. A cross-encoder reranker is the usual fix.

references.label: Reimers & Gurevych, 'Sentence-BERT'

stem: A research assistant must investigate a question across 30+ sources and synthesise findings. A single agent takes 12 minutes and often loses earlier findings by the end. When does a multi-agent design genuinely help here, and what is the main cost?

options.text: It helps because subtasks are parallel and each needs its own large context; the main cost is that coordination and token use rise sharply while shared state gets harder
options.why: This is the shape multi-agent designs actually suit — independent investigations that each fill a context and return a compact result, so the parent's context stays small. The cost is real: token consumption multiplies and any dependency between subtasks becomes a coordination problem you must build.

options.text: It helps because specialised agents with focused prompts outperform one general agent on each subtask
options.why: Role specialisation sounds compelling and is the usual justification, but the evidence for prompt-persona specialisation improving quality is weak. The real benefit here is context isolation and parallelism, not that an agent told it is a 'research specialist' reasons better.

options.text: It does not help; the answer is a longer context window and better summarisation
options.why: Compaction genuinely mitigates losing earlier findings and should be in the design. But it does nothing about the 12-minute serial runtime, which parallel sub-agents address directly — the two techniques are complements.

options.text: It helps because failures are isolated, so one agent's error does not corrupt the whole task
options.why: Isolation is a genuine secondary benefit and worth having. But sub-agents returning subtly wrong findings to a synthesiser that cannot verify them is its own failure mode, so isolation contains errors rather than preventing their effect.

explanation: Multi-agent architectures are often adopted for the wrong reason — an appealing org-chart metaphor of specialists collaborating — and the evidence for persona-based specialisation improving quality is thin. The reason that holds up is resource-shaped: when subtasks are genuinely independent and each requires substantial context, giving each its own agent means each gets a full clean window, they run in parallel, and only compact results return to the orchestrator. Broad research is the canonical fit, because investigating thirty sources is naturally parallel and no sub-result depends on another. Know the costs before committing. Token use rises steeply, often several times a single-agent run, since each sub-agent carries its own instructions and context. Coordination is real work: you must decompose the task well, and a poor decomposition produces overlapping or gap-ridden coverage. Sub-agents cannot see each other's findings, so genuinely interdependent subtasks either need a shared store or must be serialised, at which point you have lost the benefit. And debugging is much harder, since a bad final answer may come from any of a dozen parallel executions — which makes per-agent tracing non-negotiable. The heuristic worth carrying: use multi-agent when the work fans out cleanly and results merge cleanly, and prefer a single agent with good context management whenever subtasks talk to each other. Have the orchestrator verify sub-agent findings rather than trusting them, because compounding errors across agents is the failure mode that produces confident, well-structured, wrong reports.
keyTakeaway: Multi-agent earns its cost through parallelism and context isolation, not persona specialisation. If subtasks depend on each other, use one agent.

references.label: Anthropic engineering blog, 'How we built our multi-agent research system'

stem: A summarisation feature's cost is far higher than estimated. Input is about 8,000 tokens and output about 800. Which fact about pricing most likely explains the gap?

options.text: Output tokens typically cost several times more than input tokens, so a small output can dominate the bill despite being a tenth of the volume
options.why: The asymmetry is large — output is commonly three to five times the input rate — so 800 output tokens can rival or exceed 8,000 input tokens in cost. Estimating from total token counts rather than weighted rates is the standard way this goes wrong.

options.text: Input tokens are counted twice, once for prefill and once for attention over the context
options.why: Not how billing works — input tokens are counted once. This invents a mechanism rather than identifying the real asymmetry, and would not explain a large gap even if it were true.

options.text: Tokenisation is less efficient than word count suggests, so actual token usage exceeds the estimate
options.why: Real for code, non-English text and unusual identifiers, where tokens per word can be much higher than the usual heuristic. It produces a modest multiplier rather than the substantial gap the asymmetric pricing explains.

options.text: Failed requests and retries are billed, inflating the total beyond successful calls
options.why: Retries do add cost and are worth instrumenting, particularly if a validation loop retries silently. But in a working feature they are a small fraction, not the primary driver of a systematic estimation error.

explanation: The asymmetry between input and output pricing is the single most useful fact for reasoning about LLM cost, and it drives several design decisions. Because output is the expensive side, the highest-leverage optimisations reduce what the model writes. Ask for the minimal sufficient output — a label rather than a label plus justification, a diff rather than a rewritten file, structured fields rather than prose. Be deliberate about reasoning: chain-of-thought improves accuracy on hard problems and costs output tokens on every request, so use it where the accuracy matters and not by reflex. Set `max_tokens` as a real safety limit, since a runaway generation is both a cost and a latency incident. On the input side, prompt caching heavily discounts repeated prefixes, so a large stable system section is much cheaper than its raw token count suggests once caching is working. Beyond the per-request arithmetic, build the discipline of measuring cost per unit of business value — cost per ticket resolved, per document processed — rather than cost per token, because that is the number that tells you whether the feature is viable and it makes model-choice comparisons meaningful. Instrument token counts per request from day one and alert on the distribution rather than the mean, since cost incidents almost always show up as a long tail of pathological requests rather than a general drift.
keyTakeaway: Output tokens cost several times input tokens. Reduce what the model writes, cache what it reads, and measure cost per unit of business value.

references.label: Anthropic docs, 'Pricing and token counting'

stem: A coding agent's context reaches 150,000 tokens after 40 tool calls. You must compact it to continue. What should the summary preserve, and what is safe to drop?

options.text: Preserve the goal, decisions made and why, current state of the work, and open questions; drop raw tool output that has been superseded or acted upon
options.why: Decisions and their rationale are irrecoverable — nothing in the environment records why an approach was rejected — whereas file contents and directory listings can be re-read on demand and are usually stale anyway.

options.text: Preserve the most recent 20 messages verbatim and drop everything older
options.why: Recency is a poor proxy for importance: the original requirement and the key architectural decision are usually the oldest messages, and a sliding window drops exactly those while retaining incidental recent chatter.

options.text: Preserve a summary of every message proportionally, so no part of the history is lost
options.why: Uniform compression treats a rejected debugging attempt as equal in value to the requirement. It also degrades everything at once, producing a vague summary where nothing is precise enough to act on.

options.text: Preserve all tool outputs and drop the model's reasoning, since the outputs are the ground truth
options.why: Inverts the value. Tool outputs are the most re-derivable content and the largest by volume, while the reasoning contains decisions and constraints that exist nowhere else and cannot be recovered by re-running a tool.

explanation: Compaction is a lossy compression problem and the right compression ratio differs sharply by content type, so the useful question is what is recoverable. Tool output is cheap to recover — a file can be re-read, a directory relisted, a test re-run — and it is usually stale, since the agent has been changing things since. Decisions are not recoverable: nothing in the environment records that the team rejected an approach because of a constraint discovered at step 12, and losing that means the agent cheerfully re-attempts it. So structure the compacted context around what only the history knows: the original goal in the user's own terms; the decisions taken and the reasoning behind them, especially rejections; the current state of the work — files modified, what passes, what fails; and open questions or blockers. Then let the agent re-read what it needs. Two implementation points that decide whether this works. Externalise state rather than summarising it — have the agent maintain a file recording progress and decisions, so compaction reads from an authoritative artefact rather than reconstructing from a transcript, and the record survives the context entirely. And compact proactively at a threshold rather than reactively at the limit, because a compaction performed while the model is already struggling with a saturated context produces a poor summary. Worth also noting the alternative that avoids the problem: delegate self-contained subtasks to sub-agents with fresh contexts, so the parent's history never accumulates the detail in the first place.
keyTakeaway: Compact by recoverability: keep goals, decisions and rationale, drop tool output you can re-read. Externalise state to a file rather than a summary.

references.label: Anthropic engineering blog, 'Effective context engineering for AI agents'

stem: This tool is given to an agent that analyses application logs. What will go wrong?

options.text: Unbounded result size — a common query can return megabytes, blowing the context window in one call and burying the relevant lines
options.why: A single broad query against a log table can match millions of rows, and the entire serialised result is injected into the context. The agent either fails outright on a context overflow or loses the signal among thousands of near-identical entries.

options.text: The query is vulnerable to SQL injection through the `query` parameter
options.why: The parameter is passed as a bound value rather than interpolated into SQL, so this specific call is parameterised correctly. Worth staying alert to in agent tools generally, since agents do construct queries, but it is not the defect here.

options.text: `SELECT *` returns columns the agent does not need, wasting tokens
options.why: True and worth fixing — projecting only relevant columns is real token savings. It is a constant-factor improvement on top of an unbounded row count, which is the problem that actually breaks the agent.

options.text: A `LIKE` query with leading wildcards cannot use an index, so the tool will be slow
options.why: Correct about the index — a leading wildcard forces a scan and this will be slow on a large table. That is a database performance issue rather than the context-management failure that makes the tool unusable.

explanation: Every tool result is written into the context window, which makes result size a first-class design concern rather than an implementation detail. An unbounded tool is a loaded gun: one broad query and the agent's entire working memory is consumed by log lines, at which point it either errors on context overflow or, worse, continues with the signal diluted beyond recognition. Design tools to return small, high-value results. Paginate by default with an explicit limit and an offset or cursor, and return the total match count so the agent knows what it is not seeing and can refine rather than guess. Project only the fields that matter. Aggregate where the agent's actual question is aggregate — for logs, returning counts grouped by error type and a handful of representative examples is far more useful than ten thousand raw lines, and it is what a human would do. Truncate individual field values with a marker so one enormous stack trace cannot dominate. And make the truncation legible: a result that silently drops rows teaches the agent to trust an incomplete picture, whereas one that says '20 of 4,182 matches shown' prompts a narrower query. The general principle is that a tool's return value is part of its interface contract with a consumer that has a hard memory budget, so treat verbosity as a bug. Where large output genuinely must be produced, write it to a file and return the path, letting the agent read selectively rather than receiving everything at once.
keyTakeaway: Every tool result is spent context. Paginate, project, aggregate, and make truncation visible so the agent knows what it hasn't seen.

references.label: Anthropic engineering blog, 'Writing effective tools for agents'

stem: A classification prompt includes 30 few-shot examples and costs 4,000 input tokens per call at 200,000 calls/month. Accuracy is 91%. Reducing to 5 examples drops accuracy to 88%; the requirement is 85%. What is the most useful analysis?

options.text: Check whether the 30 examples cover the confusable cases and whether a well-chosen 5 beat a random 5 — example selection usually matters more than example count
options.why: Few-shot performance depends heavily on which examples are shown, especially coverage of boundary and minority classes. A curated five can approach or match thirty, so measuring selection before accepting the accuracy drop is the higher-value experiment.

options.text: Accept the 5-example version, since 88% exceeds the 85% requirement and saves substantial cost
options.why: Defensible and probably where you end up, but taking the first cheaper option without testing selection leaves accuracy on the table for free. It also spends the entire headroom above the requirement in one step, leaving no margin for drift.

options.text: Use prompt caching on the examples, which removes the cost concern entirely and lets you keep 30
options.why: Caching heavily discounts a stable prefix and is absolutely worth enabling here — it is the single easiest win. It reduces cost rather than removing it, and does nothing about the prefill latency of 4,000 tokens on every call.

options.text: Fine-tune a small model on the labelled examples, eliminating few-shot examples from the prompt
options.why: A legitimate destination once volume justifies it, and 200,000 calls a month may. It is a larger commitment with its own retraining and eval burden, so it should follow the cheap experiments rather than precede them.

explanation: Few-shot examples are context spent on teaching the task, and the return on that spend is dominated by which examples you choose rather than how many. Examples do several distinct jobs: they demonstrate the output format, they disambiguate the label boundaries, and they show how to handle edge cases. Thirty randomly chosen examples often duplicate the easy centre of each class while covering none of the confusable boundaries, whereas five chosen to sit exactly on the boundaries can teach more. So the first experiment is selection, not count: curate a set that covers every class including rare ones, includes the pairs your error analysis shows are confused, and demonstrates the format precisely. Dynamic selection is the stronger version — retrieve the k most similar labelled examples to the current input at request time, which consistently outperforms a fixed set because the examples are always relevant, at the cost of breaking prompt caching since the prefix now varies. That is a real trade to make deliberately: static examples cache well and are cheap; dynamic examples are more accurate and cost more. Two further notes. Order matters, and models show recency bias toward later examples, so put the most important ones last and keep class order balanced rather than grouped. And check for label leakage in your eval — if examples were drawn from the same pool as your eval set, your measured accuracy is optimistic and the cheaper prompt may be closer than it appears.
keyTakeaway: Which examples you show beats how many. Curate for boundaries and rare classes before trading accuracy for token count.

references.label: Liu et al., 'What Makes Good In-Context Examples for GPT-3?'

stem: An orchestrator delegates a research subtask to a sub-agent. What is the main context-engineering benefit, and what must the interface between them specify?

options.text: The sub-agent's exploration never enters the parent's context — only its conclusion does; the interface must define exactly what the sub-agent returns, since the parent cannot see its working
options.why: Isolation is the point: forty tool calls of searching happen in a context the parent never pays for. That also means the parent cannot inspect the reasoning, so the return contract has to carry everything the parent needs, including confidence and sources.

options.text: The sub-agent can use a different, cheaper model, reducing overall cost
options.why: Model routing per subtask is a genuine benefit and worth doing. It is a cost optimisation available independently of delegation, though, and not the context property that makes sub-agents structurally useful.

options.text: The sub-agent can run in parallel with other sub-agents, reducing wall-clock time
options.why: Parallelism is a real advantage of fan-out designs and often the headline reason to use them. The question asks specifically about context engineering, where the benefit is isolation rather than concurrency.

options.text: Failures in the sub-agent are isolated and do not corrupt the parent's reasoning
options.why: Partly true and a useful property, but overstated: a sub-agent that returns a confidently wrong conclusion corrupts the parent's reasoning completely, precisely because the parent cannot see how it got there.

explanation: Sub-agents are best understood as a context-management technique rather than an organisational metaphor. A research subtask might involve forty searches, each returning substantial text; run inline, that fills the parent's window with material it will never need again and degrades everything afterwards. Delegated, all of it happens in a context that is discarded, and the parent receives a paragraph. This is what makes deep, multi-step work possible within finite context, and it is why the pattern scales where a single long-running agent does not. The critical design surface is the return contract, because it is the only channel. Specify what comes back and require it explicitly: the conclusion, the evidence or sources supporting it, an explicit confidence or a statement of what could not be determined, and any assumptions made. Without that, the parent receives an assertion it cannot evaluate and cannot audit — the sub-agent's uncertainty is silently dropped and its guesses become the parent's facts. Two related habits. Have the parent verify rather than trust where the stakes justify it, spot-checking a claim against a source, because compounding unverified sub-agent conclusions is the main failure mode of multi-agent research systems. And keep the task genuinely self-contained: if the sub-agent needs to ask clarifying questions or depends on what a sibling found, the isolation that makes it valuable is exactly what makes it fail, and the work belongs in the parent.
keyTakeaway: Sub-agents keep exploration out of the parent's context. Since the parent can't see the working, the return contract must carry evidence and uncertainty.

references.label: Anthropic engineering blog, 'How we built our multi-agent research system'

stem: A prompt places a 30,000-token document first, then the instruction 'summarise the risks section in three bullets'. Output quality is inconsistent and often summarises the wrong section. What is the most likely fix?

options.text: State the task before the document as well as after, so the model reads the document knowing what it is looking for
options.why: An instruction that appears only after 30,000 tokens means the model processes the entire document with no task in mind. Framing the task first, and restating it at the end, consistently improves targeted extraction from long inputs.

options.text: Move the document after the instruction, since instructions should always come first
options.why: Half right — the instruction should appear first. Moving the document to the end forfeits prompt caching on the large stable prefix, so restating the instruction in both positions is strictly better than swapping them.

options.text: Split the document into sections and process each separately, then merge
options.why: A reasonable strategy for very long documents and it does improve focus. It is considerably more machinery than the problem needs, and it introduces a merge step that can lose cross-section context.

options.text: Lower the temperature, since inconsistency between runs indicates excessive sampling variance
options.why: Lower temperature reduces run-to-run variation and is sensible for extraction. It would make the model consistently summarise the wrong section rather than inconsistently, which is not an improvement.

explanation: Position within the prompt is a real variable, and the practical rule for long inputs is to bracket: state the task before the content and restate it after. The reason is intuitive — a model reading 30,000 tokens with no stated objective has nothing to attend selectively toward, so relevant material is processed with the same weight as everything else; whereas a model told upfront what it is looking for can carry that objective through. Restating at the end handles recency, since the final instruction is the most immediate thing before generation. This also interacts with caching in a way worth knowing: put the stable content — system instructions, the document if it recurs across requests — early so the prefix caches, and the varying instruction late. Bracketing lets you have both, with a short framing sentence at the top and the specific task at the bottom. Two adjacent techniques. Use structural delimiters so the model can tell instruction from content — XML tags or clear markdown headers around the document — which meaningfully reduces the model treating document text as instructions, and is also a mild defence against injected content in the document. And ask for the relevant excerpt before the summary: having the model first quote the risks section, then summarise it, grounds the output and makes errors visible, since you can see immediately whether it located the right passage. That decomposition is often a bigger win than any amount of prompt-position tuning.
keyTakeaway: Bracket long inputs: state the task before the content and restate it after. A model reading 30,000 tokens with no objective attends to nothing in particular.

references.label: Liu et al., 'Lost in the Middle'

stem: A support chatbot keeps the full conversation history in context. Sessions average 8 turns but some reach 60, where quality degrades and cost per turn is 15x the average. What is the best strategy?

options.text: Keep recent turns verbatim plus a running structured summary of earlier ones, and carry resolved facts as explicit state rather than as dialogue
options.why: It preserves the immediate conversational context where verbatim detail matters, while collapsing older turns into the facts that are still relevant. Extracting resolved facts into state stops the model re-deriving them from a long transcript.

options.text: Truncate to the last 10 turns, which covers the average session comfortably
options.why: Cheap and simple, but a hard cut silently drops the customer's original problem statement and any commitment made early in the conversation — exactly the content a long support session most needs to retain.

options.text: Cap sessions at 20 turns and hand off to a human agent
options.why: A sensible product control worth having for other reasons, since a 60-turn session usually signals the bot is failing. As a context strategy it avoids the problem rather than solving it, and the handoff still needs a summary.

options.text: Summarise the entire history every turn, keeping the context at a fixed small size
options.why: Repeatedly summarising a summary compounds information loss, and each pass blurs detail further. It also discards the verbatim recent turns where exact wording — the customer's last question — matters most.

explanation: Conversation history has a natural structure that a uniform policy ignores: recent turns need to be verbatim because pronouns, corrections and the immediate question depend on exact wording, while older turns matter only for the facts they established. So use a hybrid. Keep the last several turns exactly as spoken. Maintain a running summary of everything before that, updated incrementally rather than regenerated from scratch each time, which avoids the compounding degradation of summarising summaries. And separately extract durable facts into explicit state — the account ID, the order number, the problem category, what has already been tried, what was promised — because those are what the model actually needs and they are far cheaper as fields than as dialogue. That state doubles as the handoff artefact when the conversation escalates to a human, which is a real product benefit. Two things to watch. The summary must retain unresolved commitments and constraints, not just topics, since 'we agreed to refund shipping' disappearing from context is a customer-visible failure. And treat the long sessions as a signal, not just a cost: sessions reaching 60 turns are usually ones where the bot is looping or failing, so instrument turn count as a quality metric and investigate the tail rather than only optimising its token bill. Fixing the underlying failure is worth more than making it cheaper.
keyTakeaway: Recent turns verbatim, older turns as an incremental summary, established facts as explicit state — and treat very long sessions as a quality signal.

references.label: Anthropic engineering blog, 'Effective context engineering for AI agents'

stem: Why does adding a cross-encoder reranker over the top-50 retrieved chunks typically improve results more than switching to a better embedding model?

options.text: A cross-encoder scores query and document jointly, so it can model their interaction — a bi-encoder must embed each independently, before it knows the query
options.why: Embedding a document independently forces it into a fixed vector that must serve every possible future query, which is a lossy compression. A cross-encoder sees both texts together and can attend across them, capturing relevance a single similarity score cannot express.

options.text: Rerankers are trained on more data than embedding models, so they are simply more accurate
options.why: Training data volume is not the distinguishing factor, and many rerankers are built on comparable base models. The advantage is architectural — joint encoding — not a matter of scale.

options.text: Rerankers can use metadata such as recency and popularity that embeddings ignore
options.why: Ranking on metadata signals is valuable and often combined with reranking. That is a separate feature-engineering benefit, though, and a pure cross-encoder ranks on text relevance rather than metadata.

options.text: Rerankers operate on the full document rather than chunks, so they have more context
options.why: Rerankers score whatever unit you pass them, usually the same chunks the retriever returned. They typically have tighter input limits than the retrieval stage, so this inverts the actual constraint.

explanation: The distinction is bi-encoder versus cross-encoder and it explains most of the gap. A bi-encoder — what an embedding model is — maps the document to a vector at index time, with no knowledge of any query, and maps the query to a vector at search time; relevance is then a single dot product between two independently-produced compressions. That is what makes it fast enough to search millions of documents, and it is inherently lossy: the document's vector must simultaneously serve every question anyone might ask of it. A cross-encoder takes query and document together as one input and attends across both, so it can represent 'this passage answers this specific question' rather than 'this passage is about the same topic'. That is precisely the distinction that fails in practice, where topically-related-but-wrong results dominate the errors. The cost is that a cross-encoder cannot precompute anything — it must run per candidate pair — so it is unusable as a first-stage retriever and perfect as a second stage over 50 candidates. This two-stage shape, cheap recall then expensive precision, is a general pattern worth recognising: the same structure appears in classical search, recommender systems and ad ranking. Practical notes: measure recall@50 before adding a reranker, because reranking cannot recover a document retrieval never fetched; and budget the latency, since reranking 50 candidates adds real time and the right candidate count is a tunable trade against quality.
keyTakeaway: Bi-encoders compress documents before seeing the query; cross-encoders read both together. Retrieve broadly and cheaply, then rerank narrowly and well.

references.label: Nogueira & Cho, 'Passage Re-ranking with BERT'

stem: In a multi-turn RAG assistant, the user asks 'what about for enterprise customers?' after a question about refund policy. Retrieval returns irrelevant chunks. What is the fix?

options.text: Rewrite the follow-up into a standalone query using conversation context before retrieving — 'what is the refund policy for enterprise customers'
options.why: The retrieval step sees only the query string, and 'what about for enterprise customers' contains no retrievable content. Resolving the ellipsis against the conversation produces a query that actually describes what is being looked for.

options.text: Include the full conversation history in the embedding query so context is captured
options.why: Embedding a whole conversation produces a vector that averages every topic discussed, which is a muddier signal than the follow-up alone. A model rewriting the query into one clear question is far more precise than blending.

options.text: Increase top-k so the correct chunk is more likely to appear despite the poor query
options.why: Retrieving more results for a query that describes nothing in particular returns more irrelevant chunks. It dilutes the generation context while leaving the underspecified query untouched.

options.text: Add the previous question's retrieved chunks to the current context so continuity is preserved
options.why: Reasonable as a fallback and it may occasionally hit, since the refund policy chunk is likely already there. But it only works when the answer happens to live in the same chunks, and it fails as soon as the follow-up shifts to a genuinely different document.

explanation: Retrieval sees a query string, not a conversation, so any dependence on prior turns must be resolved before retrieval happens. Real follow-ups are full of ellipsis, pronouns and implicit scope — 'what about enterprise', 'and for the EU?', 'is that still true in 2025' — none of which carry retrievable content on their own. Query rewriting, sometimes called condensation, uses a cheap model call to turn the follow-up plus recent history into a standalone question, which then goes to the retriever. It is a small addition that fixes a large fraction of multi-turn RAG failures. Several related techniques share the insight that the user's words are often not the best search query. Query expansion generates several phrasings and retrieves for each, unioning the results, which improves recall when vocabulary differs between question and documents. HyDE has the model write a hypothetical answer and embeds that instead of the question, on the reasoning that a hypothetical answer looks more like the target document than a question does. Query decomposition splits a multi-part question into sub-queries and retrieves for each, which is necessary for anything requiring evidence from several documents. Two practical points: keep rewriting cheap and fast, since it sits on the critical path before retrieval, and a small model handles it well; and log the rewritten query alongside the original, because when retrieval fails you need to know whether the rewrite or the retriever was at fault — without it, you are debugging two stages at once.
keyTakeaway: The retriever never sees the conversation. Rewrite follow-ups into standalone queries first, and log both so you can tell which stage failed.

references.label: Gao et al., 'Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels (HyDE)'

stem: A policy assistant retrieves over 5 years of documents. Users report answers citing superseded policies. Roughly 30% of the corpus is outdated but historical versions must remain searchable for audit. What do you implement?

options.text: Metadata filtering with a default to current versions, plus explicit status in each chunk so the model can flag when it is citing a superseded policy
options.why: Filtering at retrieval time keeps superseded content out of normal answers, while retaining it for audit queries that opt in. Carrying status into the chunk text means that when historical content is deliberately retrieved, the model can say so rather than presenting it as current.

options.text: Delete superseded documents from the index, keeping them only in cold storage
options.why: Directly contradicts the stated audit requirement that historical versions remain searchable. It also makes the common failure — needing to know what the policy was in 2022 — impossible to serve.

options.text: Boost recent documents in the ranking so current policies score higher
options.why: Recency boosting helps on average and is a reasonable component. It is a soft preference rather than a guarantee, so a strongly-matching superseded document still surfaces, which is precisely the failure being reported.

options.text: Add the document date to each chunk so the model can judge which is current
options.why: Necessary and worth doing, but insufficient alone — a date does not tell the model whether a policy was superseded, and asking it to infer currency from dates across a mixed result set is unreliable.

explanation: Freshness is a retrieval problem before it is a generation problem, and the reliable fix is structural rather than persuasive. Store status as first-class metadata — effective date, superseded-by, current or historical — and filter on it at query time, defaulting to current. Then the normal path simply cannot return outdated content, which is a guarantee rather than a preference. Keep the historical corpus indexed and reachable through an explicit mode or an intent classifier that detects audit-style questions, so the audit requirement is met without contaminating everyday answers. Alongside filtering, carry the status into the chunk text itself, so that when a historical document is legitimately retrieved the model sees 'superseded, effective 2021-2023' as part of the content and can caveat its answer. This matters because filtering and generation are separate stages and the model has no access to your metadata unless you put it there. Two broader lessons. Corpus hygiene is an ongoing operational task rather than a one-off ingestion step: something must detect when a document is superseded and update the index, and a RAG system without that process degrades continuously as reality moves on. And this generalises past dates — tenant, region, product line, access permission and language are all the same shape, where the correct answer depends on filtering the candidate set before ranking rather than hoping relevance sorts it out. Permissions especially: retrieval must filter by what the asking user is allowed to see, and doing that in the prompt rather than the query is a security bug.
keyTakeaway: Freshness, tenancy and permissions are filters, not ranking hints. Filter before ranking, and carry status into the chunk so the model can caveat.

references.label: Barnett et al., 'Seven Failure Points When Engineering a RAG System'

stem: This is the main loop of a production agent. What is missing?

options.text: No bound on iterations, tokens, wall time or spend — a looping agent runs until something external kills it, and nothing detects repeated identical actions
options.why: The only exit is the model choosing to stop, which a stuck agent never does. Without step, token, time and cost ceilings plus loop detection, a single bad task can consume unbounded money and hold resources indefinitely.

options.text: Tool execution errors are not caught, so an exception escapes the loop and kills the agent
options.why: A genuine robustness gap — `execute` should catch and return the error as a tool result so the model can recover. It causes an abrupt failure rather than the unbounded consumption that makes this loop dangerous in production.

options.text: Tool calls are executed sequentially rather than in parallel, making the agent slow
options.why: Parallelising independent tool calls is a worthwhile latency optimisation. It is a performance concern, not a correctness or safety one, and it does not affect whether the loop terminates.

options.text: The message list grows without bound, eventually exceeding the context window
options.why: Real and important — this loop has no compaction, so long tasks will hit the window. It surfaces as a clear API error, though, whereas the missing bounds allow silent, expensive, indefinite running.

explanation: Every agent loop needs explicit termination conditions, because the model deciding to stop is the one exit path you cannot rely on — a confused agent will happily retry variations of a failing action forever. Bound it on four axes, since each catches a different pathology: a maximum step count, which catches straightforward looping; a token budget, which catches steps that individually grow enormous; wall-clock time, which catches a slow tool holding the loop open; and cost, which is the one finance will ask about and the only one denominated in something the business understands. Add loop detection on top of the counters — hash the tool call and its arguments, and if the same call repeats several times with no state change, break out rather than waiting for the step limit, because a fast tight loop can burn a step budget in seconds. When any bound trips, do not fail silently: return partial results with a clear reason, log the full trace, and surface it as a metric, because bound-hits are your primary signal that a task class is unsolvable or a tool is broken. Two further points. Make the bounds configurable per task type, since a quick lookup and a deep research task have legitimately different budgets, and a single global limit will be simultaneously too tight and too loose. And catch tool exceptions and feed the error text back as a tool result rather than letting it escape — an agent that sees 'connection refused' can adapt, whereas an agent that crashes cannot, and this single change converts a large share of hard failures into recoveries.
keyTakeaway: Never let the model be the only exit. Bound steps, tokens, time and cost, detect repeated actions, and feed tool errors back rather than crashing.

references.label: Anthropic engineering blog, 'Building effective agents'

stem: A code-writing agent completes tasks correctly about 55% of the time. Adding a step where it reviews its own output before finishing raises this to 62%. Adding a step where it runs the test suite and iterates on failures raises it to 84%. Why the difference?

options.text: The test suite is an external, objective signal the model cannot rationalise; self-review reuses the same reasoning that produced the error
options.why: Self-critique is correlated with the original generation — the model's blind spots apply equally to producing and reviewing. An executable check provides ground truth from outside the model, which is why grounded verification dominates introspective verification.

options.text: Running tests gives the model more context about the codebase, improving its understanding
options.why: Extra context is a minor side benefit. The decisive factor is that test output is a verdict the model did not generate, not that it is additional information to read.

options.text: Self-review is limited by the model's context window, while test output is compact
options.why: Compactness is incidental and test output can be verbose. The difference persists regardless of length, because it is about the independence of the signal rather than its size.

options.text: Tests catch runtime errors while self-review only catches logical errors
options.why: Describes a difference in coverage that is partly real, but understates it. Tests also catch logical errors when they assert on behaviour, and the deeper point is the source of the judgement, not its category.

explanation: The general principle is that verification is only as good as its independence from generation. Asking a model to check its own work uses the same weights, the same context and the same misunderstandings that produced the output, so it reliably catches surface slips — a syntax error, an obviously missing case — and reliably misses the errors that stem from misreading the requirement, because the reviewer misreads it identically. Grounded verification breaks that correlation by consulting something outside the model: a test suite, a compiler, a type checker, a linter, a schema validator, a database constraint, an API that rejects malformed input. Each returns a verdict the model cannot argue with, and each converts a silent wrong answer into a signal the agent can act on. This is why the highest-leverage investment in agent reliability is usually not a better model or a better prompt but better executable feedback: making the test suite fast and comprehensive, adding type annotations, tightening schemas. It is also why agentic coding works far better in codebases with good tests, which is a fact worth telling your team. Two extensions. Where no executable check exists, an independent model call with a different prompt and no sight of the original reasoning is a weaker but real substitute — the independence is what matters, so do not simply ask 'is this right?' in the same conversation. And design the loop so failures feed back as specific, actionable text: 'test_refund_partial failed: expected 40, got 0' produces a fix, whereas 'tests failed' produces a guess.
keyTakeaway: Verification must be independent of generation. An executable check beats self-critique, which shares the blind spots that caused the error.

references.label: Huang et al., 'Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet'

stem: How does evaluating an agent differ from evaluating a single-turn LLM call, and what must you measure that end-to-end success rate hides?

options.text: Agents take a trajectory, so you must measure per-step quality — tool selection, argument correctness, recovery from errors — since many paths reach the same outcome and success rate cannot tell you why it failed
options.why: A pass/fail on the final answer collapses a long execution into one bit, giving no way to distinguish a wrong tool choice from a good plan defeated by a broken tool. Step-level metrics tell you which part of the system to fix.

options.text: Agents are non-deterministic, so evaluations must be run many times and averaged
options.why: Repeated runs are genuinely necessary — agent variance is high and a single run tells you little. But that is a statistical requirement that applies to single-turn calls too, not the structural difference trajectories introduce.

options.text: Agents are expensive to run, so evaluation must use a smaller sample than single-turn evaluation
options.why: Cost is a real practical constraint on agent eval suites and does force smaller sets. It is a budget consideration rather than a difference in what you should be measuring.

options.text: Agents interact with external systems, so evaluation requires a full staging environment
options.why: Environment fidelity matters and reproducible fixtures or recorded tools are important for stable evals. It describes an infrastructure requirement rather than the measurement gap the question asks about.

explanation: A single-turn call has one input and one output, so grading the output is grading the system. An agent produces a trajectory — a sequence of decisions, tool calls, observations and recoveries — and the final answer is a lossy summary of all of it. That creates two problems for pass/fail evaluation. It gives no diagnostic signal: a 55% success rate tells you nothing about whether failures came from poor tool selection, malformed arguments, giving up too early, or an environment problem. And it hides process quality: an agent that reaches the right answer after 40 flailing steps scores identically to one that took 4, though the first is far more expensive and far more fragile. So measure the trajectory. Tool selection accuracy — did it choose the right tool for the step? Argument validity — were the parameters well-formed and sensible? Recovery rate — when a tool returned an error, did it adapt or repeat? Efficiency — steps and tokens per successful task, which is your cost driver and an early warning of degradation. And termination behaviour — how often it hits a bound rather than finishing. Two practical notes. Build the eval set from real trajectories, including failed ones, and stabilise the environment with recorded or mocked tools so runs are comparable; otherwise you are measuring your dependencies' variance alongside the agent's. And run each case several times and report the distribution, because agent variance is wide enough that a single run per case will mislead you about whether a change helped.
keyTakeaway: Grade the trajectory, not just the outcome. Tool choice, argument validity, recovery rate and steps-per-success tell you what to fix; a success rate doesn't.

references.label: Yao et al., 'ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models'

stem: An agent feature costs about $400/day for two weeks, then $9,000 on a single day with no traffic increase. What is the most likely mechanism, and what control was missing?

options.text: A small number of tasks entered long loops — cost per task is heavy-tailed, so the mean is set by the tail; per-task budget caps and alerting on the distribution were missing
options.why: Agent cost per task varies by orders of magnitude, so a handful of pathological runs dominates the bill without changing traffic volume. A per-task ceiling bounds the worst case, which an aggregate daily budget alert cannot do until the money is already spent.

options.text: A model version change increased per-token pricing, and the model alias was not pinned
options.why: Unpinned aliases are a real hazard and worth fixing. A pricing or model change would produce a step change that persists, not a single-day spike that implies something transient.

options.text: Prompt caching stopped working, so input tokens were billed at full price
options.why: A cache going cold is a genuine and easily-missed cost regression, and worth alerting on. Losing cache discounts produces a multiple of a few, not the more than twentyfold spike described.

options.text: A retry loop in the application re-submitted failed requests, multiplying API calls
options.why: Retry storms do multiply cost and are worth bounding with a retry budget. This is close to correct, but attributes the loop to the application layer when the characteristic agent failure is the agent's own reasoning loop.

explanation: Agent cost distributions are heavy-tailed in a way that single-call systems are not, and reasoning in means will mislead you. Most tasks finish in a handful of steps; a few enter loops, retry the same failing tool repeatedly, or explore enormous search spaces, and those consume hundreds of times the median. The mean is therefore governed by the tail, and a day with a few dozen pathological runs looks like a billing incident with no change in traffic. The control that actually bounds this is a per-task budget, enforced inside the loop: track cumulative tokens and cost for the task, and terminate with a partial result when the ceiling is reached. That converts an unbounded liability into a known worst case you can multiply by task volume and put in a capacity plan. Aggregate alerting is necessary but insufficient — a daily spend alert tells you after the money is gone, and an hourly one still permits a very expensive hour. Around that, build the observability to explain it: record cost per task and alert on the p99 rather than the mean, since the mean moves late and the tail moves first; log the trajectory for any task that exceeds a threshold, so you can see what it was looping on; and track steps-per-task as a leading indicator, because step count rises before the bill does. Two supporting habits. Set the per-task limit from the observed distribution — a limit at several times p99 rarely fires on legitimate work — and make hitting it a monitored event, since a rising rate of budget termination is usually a broken tool rather than harder tasks.
keyTakeaway: Agent cost per task is heavy-tailed, so the tail sets the bill. Enforce a per-task budget inside the loop and alert on p99 cost, not the mean.

references.label: Anthropic docs, 'Token counting and usage'

stem: An agent's tool call fails with a validation error. Three designs are proposed: abort the task; retry the identical call 3 times with backoff; or return the error text to the model and let it try again. The agent runs 20,000 tasks/day and each model call costs roughly 4 cents. Which, and why?

options.text: Return the error text — a validation failure is deterministic, so an identical retry fails identically, but a specific error message lets the model correct its arguments
options.why: Validation errors are caused by the input, so repeating the input reproduces the failure exactly. Feeding back what was wrong gives the model the one thing it needs to construct a valid call, and this recovery path resolves a large share of tool failures.

options.text: Abort the task, since a validation error indicates the model has misunderstood and further attempts will compound the error
options.why: Discards a recoverable situation. Models correct malformed arguments reliably when told what was wrong, and aborting on first error makes the agent far more brittle than the underlying capability warrants.

options.text: Retry three times with backoff, which handles both transient and permanent failures uniformly
options.why: Uniform retry is right for transient faults and useless for deterministic ones — three identical validation failures cost three round trips and produce the same result. Treating all errors the same wastes budget on the ones that cannot succeed.

options.text: Return the error text but cap attempts at two, then abort to avoid an expensive loop
options.why: Very close, and capping attempts is genuinely necessary. It is a refinement of returning the error rather than an alternative, and fixing the cap at two is arbitrary when the right bound depends on the task and the error class.

explanation: The distinction that matters is between transient and deterministic failures, and they need opposite treatments. A transient failure — timeout, connection reset, 503, rate limit — is caused by the environment and an identical retry with backoff is exactly right. A deterministic failure — validation error, not found, permission denied, malformed query — is caused by the input, so retrying unchanged is guaranteed to fail again and simply burns budget. Deterministic failures need the model in the loop: return the error as a tool result, phrased so it teaches. 'Invalid date format: expected YYYY-MM-DD, received 12/03/2024' produces a correct retry; 'validation error' produces a guess. This is the single highest-return investment in agent tooling, because well-written errors convert a large fraction of hard failures into successful recoveries at the cost of one extra step. Build the classification into the tool layer so it is consistent: catch exceptions, decide transient or deterministic, retry the former internally with backoff, and surface the latter to the model with actionable detail. Then bound the recovery loop — count consecutive failures on the same tool and stop after a small number, because an agent that cannot fix its call after three informative errors is unlikely to fix it on the fourth, and that is a signal the tool or the task is wrong. Log those cases; a rising rate of unrecovered errors on one tool is the clearest possible indication that its schema or its description needs work.
keyTakeaway: Retry transient failures in code; hand deterministic ones back to the model with an error message specific enough to act on.

references.label: Anthropic engineering blog, 'Writing effective tools for agents'

stem: An internal agent helps 40 on-call engineers investigate incidents across 12 services. It needs to read logs, query the metrics store, and read the code repository. A proposal grants it the on-call engineer's own credentials for convenience, since they are already authenticated. What should you argue?

options.text: Give the agent its own identity with exactly the read scopes it needs — inheriting a human's credentials means any compromise or injection acts with that human's full authority, and the audit log attributes it to them
options.why: A separate identity bounds what a compromised or manipulated agent can do, and it makes actions distinguishable in the audit trail. Borrowing a human's credentials grants every permission they hold, including write and production access the task never needs.

options.text: The proposal is acceptable for an internal tool, since the engineer is present and supervising the agent's actions
options.why: Supervision is not a permission boundary — an engineer watching a stream of tool calls will not catch a subtly wrong one, and 'internal' does not mean the log content the agent reads is trustworthy.

options.text: Grant the credentials but log every action the agent takes for later review
options.why: Logging is necessary and gives you forensics, but it is a detective control rather than a preventive one. It tells you what happened after an over-privileged agent has already done it.

options.text: Require the engineer to approve each tool call before it executes
options.why: Appropriate for consequential write actions, and worth having there. Applied to every read in an incident investigation it destroys the tool's usefulness and induces approval fatigue, which makes the eventual important prompt get waved through.

explanation: Agent identity is a security design decision, and the convenient answer is the wrong one. An agent operating with a human's credentials has every permission that human holds — production write access, deployment rights, customer data, whatever else has accumulated in their account over years — while its task needs three read scopes. That gap is the blast radius of any compromise, and compromise here does not require an attacker: an incident agent reads logs, and logs contain text written by users and third parties, which is a prompt injection surface. Content that arrives in a log line can attempt to steer the agent, and an over-privileged agent gives that content real power. Give the agent its own service identity with narrowly scoped read-only permissions, ideally issued per session and short-lived. That bounds the damage, makes actions attributable in audit logs — which matters enormously during a post-incident review, where 'was that the engineer or the agent?' must have an answer — and lets you revoke the agent without touching anyone's account. Layer on top: scope by resource as well as action, so it reads the log streams and repositories relevant to the service rather than everything; require human approval specifically for writes and irreversible actions, keeping reads frictionless so the tool remains useful; rate-limit and monitor for anomalous access patterns. The transferable question is the one to bring to any agent design: assume an attacker fully controls the model's output, then ask what the credentials permit. If that answer is unacceptable, the credentials are wrong — not the model.
keyTakeaway: Give agents their own scoped, short-lived identity. Borrowing a human's credentials grants every permission they have and destroys attribution.

references.label: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, 'Excessive Agency'

stem: A RAG assistant over a company wiki starts giving strange answers to unrelated questions. Investigation finds a wiki page containing text addressed to the assistant. Anyone at the company can edit the wiki. What is the correct assessment?

options.text: The retrieval corpus is an untrusted input channel — any content that can enter the index can influence every user's answers, so corpus write access is effectively prompt-authoring access
options.why: Retrieved chunks enter the same token stream as instructions, so whoever can write to the corpus can shape the assistant's behaviour for everyone. Wiki edit rights and prompt-modification rights turn out to be the same privilege, which nobody intended.

options.text: This is a content moderation problem — scan the wiki for prompt-like text and remove it
options.why: Detection helps and is worth doing as one layer, but injection is semantic and paraphrasable, so no scanner catches every phrasing. Treating it as moderation also misses that the underlying issue is a privilege boundary.

options.text: The system prompt should instruct the model to ignore instructions found in retrieved documents
options.why: A reasonable layer that raises the bar against casual cases, and worth including. It is a probabilistic mitigation inside the model, so it cannot be relied on against someone iterating on phrasings.

options.text: This is low severity since it is an internal wiki and the editor was likely experimenting rather than attacking
options.why: The intent of this particular editor is not the point. The finding is that a control does not exist, and internal systems face compromised accounts, contractors, and honest mistakes that produce the same effect.

explanation: Indirect prompt injection is the version of this problem that surprises teams, because the attack does not come through the user's message at all. Anything the system retrieves — wiki pages, tickets, emails, web content, PDFs, code comments — is written into the model's context alongside your instructions, and the model has no reliable way to treat one as data and the other as command. So the practical realisation is that write access to the retrieval corpus is write access to the prompt, for every user of the assistant. That reframes the fix as a permissions and architecture question. Control what enters the index: treat ingestion as a trust boundary, prefer curated or reviewed sources for anything the assistant will present authoritatively, and record provenance per chunk so you can attribute and remove. Constrain what the assistant can do: an assistant that only answers questions has a much smaller injection payoff than one that can also send email or file tickets, so scope tools tightly and require confirmation for actions. Segregate trust levels, keeping untrusted retrieved content out of any context that carries privileged tools. And make it observable: cite sources in every answer, which lets users notice when an answer comes from an odd place, and log retrieved chunk IDs so you can trace a bad answer back to its source — which is exactly how this was found. Add the system prompt instruction and a detection scan as layers, while being clear with stakeholders that neither is a boundary.
keyTakeaway: Whoever can write to your retrieval corpus can write to your prompt. Control ingestion, scope tools, record provenance, and cite sources.

stem: An agent manages calendar and email for 2,000 internal users. Product wants it to act autonomously to keep the feature useful, and is worried that confirmation prompts on every action will make people turn it off. Which actions should require confirmation, and what principle decides?

options.text: Reversibility and externality — actions that cannot be undone or that others observe need confirmation; internal, reversible ones do not
options.why: A draft can be rewritten and a moved meeting can be moved back, but a sent email cannot be unsent and a cancelled interview has already reached the candidate. Those two axes sort the action space without needing a case-by-case rulebook.

options.text: Any action that writes rather than reads should require confirmation
options.why: Too coarse in both directions: it interrupts for harmless writes like drafting or tagging, producing approval fatigue, while treating a reversible internal write the same as sending a message to a customer.

options.text: Actions should require confirmation when the model's confidence is below a threshold
options.why: Confidence is a useful additional signal but a poor primary gate, since models are confidently wrong and a high-confidence irreversible action is exactly the dangerous case. It also makes the safety property depend on a calibration you do not control.

options.text: Actions affecting other people's calendars need confirmation; the user's own data does not
options.why: Captures the externality half correctly and misses reversibility — deleting the user's own email permanently is irreversible and consequential even though nobody else sees it.

explanation: Two questions sort almost any agent action. Can it be undone? And does anyone outside the system see it? Reversible and internal — drafting, tagging, searching, moving a private event — should run without friction, because that is where the value of autonomy lives and interrupting there trains users to click through. Irreversible or externally visible — sending, deleting permanently, cancelling, declining on the user's behalf, anything that reaches another person — needs a confirmation showing exactly what will happen, because that is where a mistake cannot be walked back. The design goal is to keep the total number of confirmations low enough that each one is genuinely read; a system that asks constantly gets approved reflexively, at which point the control has been removed while appearing to exist. Two techniques extend this well. Where possible, convert irreversible actions into reversible ones and drop the confirmation: a send-delay queue makes 'send' undoable for thirty seconds, soft-delete makes deletion recoverable, and staging a draft rather than sending removes the externality. That is usually better than adding a prompt, because it preserves autonomy. And design the confirmation itself to be decidable — show the recipient, the subject, and the body, not 'the agent wants to call send_email', since a user cannot evaluate a request they cannot see. Finally, log every action with the context that triggered it, since the actions that most need auditing are precisely the ones that reached other people.
keyTakeaway: Gate on reversibility and externality. Better still, engineer irreversible actions into reversible ones — undo beats a confirmation prompt.

stem: A support assistant processes tickets containing customer names, emails and occasionally payment details. What is the most important architectural control?

options.text: Minimise what reaches the model at all — redact or tokenise sensitive fields before they enter the prompt, since anything sent is logged, cached and potentially retained downstream
options.why: Every layer between you and the model may persist the prompt: your own logs, traces, eval datasets and the provider's systems. Data that never enters the prompt cannot leak through any of them, which is the only control that holds across all of them.

options.text: Use a provider contract that guarantees data is not retained or used for training
options.why: Contractual controls are genuinely important and you should have them. They govern one party's behaviour while doing nothing about your own observability stack, which is usually where prompts actually accumulate in searchable form.

options.text: Add output filtering to detect and redact PII before responses reach the user
options.why: Worth having as a layer, particularly against the model echoing data from one context into another. It protects the output path only, leaving the prompt, the traces and the eval datasets full of raw personal data.

options.text: Encrypt prompts in transit and at rest throughout the pipeline
options.why: Table stakes that every system should have, and it protects against interception and stolen storage. It does nothing about authorised access to logs, which is the realistic exposure path for prompt data.

explanation: The instinct that serves you best is data minimisation, because a prompt is not a transient message — it is written to your application logs, your tracing backend, your prompt-and-response store, any eval dataset built from production traffic, and the provider's systems. Each is a copy with its own access controls and retention, and each is usually searchable by more people than the original ticket was. So the strongest control is to reduce what enters that pipeline. Redact or tokenise before the prompt is built: replace names and emails with stable placeholders, keep the mapping in your own system, and substitute back on output if needed — the model usually reasons perfectly well about `CUSTOMER_1` and `EMAIL_1`, since the identity rarely matters to the task. Payment details should never enter a prompt at all; there is no task that needs them and their presence brings compliance scope you do not want. Around that, build the supporting controls: configure structured logging to exclude prompt bodies or to log redacted versions, since the default of logging everything is how this goes wrong; set retention limits deliberately rather than inheriting your platform's defaults; scrub eval datasets, which are the most-copied and least-governed artefacts in most AI systems; and check the provider's retention and training terms. Two further habits: make redaction a library everyone uses rather than a per-service reimplementation, and add a test that asserts known PII patterns never appear in outbound prompts, because this is the sort of control that silently regresses when someone adds a new field.
keyTakeaway: A prompt is copied into logs, traces and eval sets. Redact before the prompt is built — that is the only control that holds across every copy.
